messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 40
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Software Engineer
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 37

Ahmed, a forty-year-old software engineer of Middle Eastern descent, lives in California with his wife. His life took an unexpected and harrowing turn during the recent series of powerful earthquakes that struck the region last year. While these natural disasters are not uncommon in this part of the world, Ahmed experienced one particular quake as especially traumatic. The night of the earthquake was like many others for him; he had been working late on a project at home when his wife called out to him to feel the first tremors. Initially, they both thought it would pass quickly and tried to remain calm. However, within minutes, the shaking grew stronger and more violent than anything Ahmed had ever experienced. Panic set in as the walls of their apartment began to crack, and he could hear items falling from shelves throughout the building. Ahmed vividly recalls his heart racing as they both rushed to a safer spot away from windows and heavy furniture. He still shudders remembering how his body shook with fear as they huddled together, trying to protect themselves. The momentary silence after the quake was almost worse than the shaking itself, filled only by the sounds of shattered glass and creaking structures. Since that night, Ahmed has found himself struggling to cope with intrusive memories and flashbacks of the earthquake. Sometimes, even small tremors or vibrations can trigger vivid recollections of the event, making him feel as though he’s right back there again. These episodes are often accompanied by a sense of dread and intense anxiety, leaving him feeling drained and on edge for hours afterward. At work, Ahmed's performance has noticeably dipped due to his inability to focus. His mind frequently wanders back to that night, replaying the terrifying moments over and over. He finds himself spacing out during meetings or while coding, which leads to mistakes he would normally catch immediately. Ahmed’s boss has noticed a decline in his usual meticulous attention to detail, but Ahmed is hesitant to reveal the underlying cause of his difficulties. Outside of work, Ahmed has also become more isolated from his friends and family. He avoids any activities that might expose him to loud noises or sudden movements, fearing they could trigger another flashback. This includes going to movies or concerts, which used to be a regular part of his social life. His wife notices how withdrawn he’s become and is worried about the toll this is taking on their relationship. Ahmed finds solace in routine and order, often spending evenings organizing and tidying up their home. He hopes that by maintaining control over these aspects of his environment, he can mitigate some of the anxiety he feels. However, even with these efforts, he frequently wakes up from nightmares where the earthquake is happening all over again. His wife has encouraged him to speak with a therapist about what happened and how he’s feeling since the event. Ahmed knows she means well but remains hesitant, fearing that seeking help will make him appear weak or unable to handle his emotions. Despite this internal struggle, Ahmed acknowledges that something needs to change in order for him to regain some sense of normalcy. Ahmed's experience with the earthquake has left indelible marks on his psyche and daily life. The lingering fear, coupled with the intrusive memories and avoidance behaviors, continues to shape how he interacts with the world around him. While Ahmed remains committed to finding a way forward, navigating these challenges is both daunting and exhausting.
